evaluation.positioning_hook: A resort manager and her stranded guests must survive a mountain storm when shadow creatures emerge from the dark and hunt anything the light can’t reach.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and genre-clean: a contained survival horror setup with a simple, visual rule set around light and darkness. The audience lane is real and commercial, though it skews genre-specific rather than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages with Cole’s disappearance on the mountain road and then the resort-wide vanishings. The script makes the threat and the survival rule clear early: stay in the light, or get taken.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Deanna has a strong emotional center, and the ensemble gives the script multiple playable adult roles with distinct textures. The characters are functional and sympathetic, though the script leans more on group survival than on deeply surprising individual arcs.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The shadow-creature mythology, the light-based vulnerability, and the mountain-resort isolation give the script a fresh monster-movie wrapper. It’s not radically experimental, but the execution has enough specificity to stand apart from generic creature features.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps the pressure on with disappearances, escalating attacks, and repeated reversals that force the group to adapt. It does occasionally pause for exposition and grief-processing, but the engine remains active and readable.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of light as both weapon and shelter is immediately intuitive, and the resort setting gives the horror a practical, story-generating container. The mythology around Nalusa Falaya and the portal adds a distinctive cultural texture without overcomplicating the premise.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The resort has a usable ecosystem of staff, guests, maintenance, and ski patrol, which gives the story a lived-in operational feel. The world is specific enough to generate scenes and tactics, though it remains primarily a survival container rather than a deeply layered social world.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a clear blend of dread, banter, and family-drama warmth, with humor used to keep the ensemble human under pressure. The tonal identity is consistent and accessible, even if it sits in a familiar horror-adventure register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The grief threads around Deanna, Ellen, Sooni, and Kelvin suggest more emotional material than the monster plot alone requires. That said, the script mostly states its emotional wounds directly rather than building a lot of subtextual mystery.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is one of the script’s strongest assets: Deanna/Maya, Deanna/Kelvin, Ellen/Aurora, Sooni/Hector, and Gage/Aurora all generate usable scene energy. The ensemble is not just presentational; it creates a real survival system where shifting alliances and caregiving matter.

lead_characters.name: Deanna Hughes
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 20s, Caucasian, working-class resort employee, married
lead_characters.hook: Deanna is the emotional anchor of the script: competent, warm, and quietly shattered by loss. She’s still showing up for work, still managing guests, and still trying to hold her marriage together even as Cole disappears and old guilt over her nephew’s death keeps resurfacing. Her locket and her habit of deflecting pain with humor give her a lived-in, human quality that makes her easy to root for.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Emily Blunt in A Quiet Place — a grounded, resourceful woman carrying fear, love, and command in the same frame. It gives an actor the chance to play leadership under pressure, grief without speeches, and action that grows out of emotional responsibility.

lead_characters.name: Maya Williams
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 50s, African American, resort manager, maternal presence
lead_characters.hook: Maya is the resort’s steady hand and the script’s best source of adult authority with a sense of humor. She’s practical, affectionate, and unflappable until the situation becomes impossible, at which point her warmth turns into steel. She feels like the kind of manager who knows everyone’s business and everyone’s pain.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Octavia Spencer in Ma or Melissa McCarthy in Can You Ever Forgive Me? a chance to own scenes through wit, authority, and emotional surprise. It offers a veteran actor a rich supporting turn with real command and late-story heroism.

lead_characters.name: Sooni Butler
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 30s, Native American, housekeeping lead, physically capable
lead_characters.hook: Sooni is the script’s most practical survivor: observant, tough, and culturally grounded without being reduced to exposition. She starts as the person who knows the folklore, then becomes one of the people who can actually fight back. Her ex-husband and sons give her a strong offscreen emotional life that keeps her from feeling like a utility character.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting-territory for someone who wants the grounded resilience of Tantoo Cardinal in Wind River or Amber Midthunder in Prey. The role offers physical survival beats, emotional restraint, and a meaningful cultural perspective.

lead_characters.name: Ellen Davenport
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 40s, Caucasian, upper-working/middle-class guest, mother
lead_characters.hook: Ellen starts as a sharp-edged, overextended mother and becomes one of the story’s most emotionally legible survivors. Her irritation masks fear, guilt, and a real need to protect her children, and the script gives her a credible arc from denial to action. She’s prickly in a way that makes her feel specific rather than generic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the Frances McDormand in Three Billboards thing: abrasive, wounded, then unexpectedly moving. It gives a performer a chance to play maternal ferocity and collapse in equal measure.

lead_characters.name: Hector Sanchez
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, Latino, security guard, physically fit
lead_characters.hook: Hector is the young guy with charm, competence, and a real emotional core, not just comic relief. He flirts, jokes, and keeps moving, but he also carries a protective instinct that makes his later material land harder. His relationship with Maya gives him a surrogate-family dimension that helps the ensemble feel alive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of breakout supporting role that gave Diego Luna in Rogue One or Xolo Maridueña in Cobra Kai a chance to be likable, capable, and emotionally accessible. It offers action, banter, and a genuine sacrifice beat.

lead_characters.name: Kelvin Byrd
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s, African American, former football player, guest
lead_characters.hook: Kelvin is a big, physically imposing guy with a soft center and a lot of grief under the surface. He’s useful in a crisis, but the script also lets him be vulnerable about Nahla, which keeps him from reading as just the strong one. His anger and tenderness both play well.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded authority of Winston Duke in Us with the emotional access of a family drama lead. It’s a strong showcase for physical presence plus grief-driven vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: Aurora Davenport
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 14, Caucasian, teenage daughter, scar on cheek
lead_characters.hook: Aurora is angry, defensive, and smart enough to weaponize cruelty when she feels powerless. The scar on her face gives her an immediate visual identity, and the script uses her hostility to mask fear and hurt. She’s a believable teen with enough edge to register beyond stock horror-kid behavior.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can do for a young actor what Hailee Steinfeld in True Grit did: toughness, pain, and attitude in one package. It gives a teenager a real emotional and physical survival arc.

lead_characters.name: Gage
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 8, African American, child, bookish and fearful of the dark
lead_characters.hook: Gage is the script’s emotional and mythological key: a frightened, bookish kid whose fear of the dark turns out to be justified. He’s vulnerable without being passive, and the story smartly lets his knowledge of the folklore become useful. He also gives the ensemble a child’s-eye urgency that keeps the stakes personal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that can become memorable the way Jacob Tremblay in Room did: fear, intelligence, and emotional truth. It gives a young performer a chance to be the audience’s surrogate and the story’s hidden expert.

lead_characters.name: Nahla Byrd
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, Indian American, guest, wife and mother
lead_characters.hook: Nahla is a warm, brief presence whose disappearance gives the story one of its strongest emotional jolts. Even with limited page time, she reads as a real person with a marriage, a body, and a life beyond the plot mechanics. Her absence matters because the script makes Kelvin’s grief feel specific.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but emotionally loaded role in the vein of the kind of part that lets an actor make a lasting impression in a few scenes, like the early family material in The Mist. It’s a strong brief-turn showcase if cast with someone who can make the loss land.

casting_characteristics: one teen girl with a visible facial scar
ensemble of adult roles across late 20s to mid 50s
specific Native American supporting role with cultural authenticity considerations

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: roughly 60/40 interior-heavy with recurring exterior mountain-road and snowfield sequences

technical.vfx_details: Primarily creature work, shadow integration, disappearance effects, and some environmental enhancement for storm/snow conditions; no large-scale digital worldbuilding.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical creature attacks, frostbite makeup, breakaway effects, fire/flare beats, snow and ice effects, vehicle impacts, and window interaction gags.

rights_flags.detail: Nalusa Falaya / shadow-creature folklore references and the Native American folklore book used as plot material

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer original, specialty theatrical, or genre-label theatrical with broad home-viewing upside

budget.note: The resort, snowstorm, creature effects, night work, and multiple vehicle/stunt beats keep this above a simple contained indie, but it remains scopeable without tentpole escalation.

casting.note: Deanna needs a strong emotional lead, and the ensemble depends on several specific age/identity slots, including a Native American supporting role and a child performer who can carry fear and exposition.

development.note: The mythology is clear enough to play, but the script will need careful handling around the folklore material and the balance between creature survival and family-drama emotion.

comp_set.title: The Lodge
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shared snowbound isolation, family trauma, and a pressure-cooker survival setup that turns a remote location into a psychological trap.

comp_set.title: The Mist
comp_set.why_it_comps: Ensemble survival under siege with creatures outside and interpersonal fracture inside, plus a strong contained-location escalation pattern.

comp_set.title: The Descent
comp_set.why_it_comps: A group of women and allies fighting an unseen threat in a confined, dark environment where visibility is the central survival rule.

comp_set.title: Prey
comp_set.why_it_comps: Creature-feature momentum with a clear tactical rule set, a survivalist lead, and a fresh cultural texture around the threat.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre fans who want a clean, high-concept creature feature with an emotional ensemble and a strong female survival lead.
audience_target.demographics: Adults 18-49, slightly male-skewing on the horror side but with strong female appeal through the ensemble and mother/child dynamics.

budget_tier.note: Contained resort setting, limited creature design, practical snow work, and a manageable number of recurring locations keep this in indie-feature territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where a clear monster rule, a contained location, and a strong emotional lead can sell the package without needing franchise-scale spend. The ensemble and winter setting make it especially attractive to buyers looking for a winter-release genre title with a clean hook.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The mythology is serviceable for this story, but no supporting character or world element is developed as a clean sequel/spinoff anchor.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The light rule is instantly cinematic.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a clean, marketable survival mechanic that audiences can understand in one image and trailers can sell in one beat. Buyers looking for a high-concept creature feature will immediately see the hook and the visual language.
strengths.evidence: The creatures burn in light, retreat from flashlights, and become lethal the moment the characters lose illumination.

strengths.what_it_means: Multiple adult relationships generate scene value, which makes the script easier to cast, easier to pace, and more emotionally durable than a single-protagonist monster movie. That broadens the buyer conversation to actors and directors who want a real company of roles, not just a lead vehicle.
strengths.evidence: Deanna/Maya, Sooni/Hector, Ellen/Aurora, and Kelvin/Maya each have distinct chemistry and recurring emotional beats.

strengths.what_it_means: A mountain lodge gives the film a contained production footprint while still offering multiple playable spaces, from lobby to pool to cabins to maintenance areas. That combination is attractive to buyers because it supports suspense without requiring a sprawling budget.
strengths.evidence: The script repeatedly uses the lobby, pool, laundry, cabins, guard shack, and road access points as tactical spaces.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The grief engine gives the horror weight.
strengths.what_it_means: The monster plot is tied to loss, guilt, and family fracture, which makes the scares feel emotionally motivated rather than arbitrary. That helps the script play above disposable creature-feature level for streamers and genre labels that want feeling with the thrills.
strengths.evidence: Deanna’s guilt over Billy, Ellen’s family strain, Sooni’s ex and sons, and Kelvin’s grief over Nahla all feed the emotional stakes.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final act turns civilians into a team.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie earns a satisfying survival payoff by converting the group from frightened bystanders into an organized, light-based defense unit. That kind of collective victory plays well with audiences and gives the ending a crowd-pleasing lift.
strengths.evidence: The Molotov cocktail assault, the snowmobile headlights, and the ski patrol rescue all build to a communal survival climax.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, sellable contained creature feature with a strong visual rule, a real ensemble engine, and a production footprint that stays inside indie-feature economics. The emotional grief layer gives it more weight than a standard monster movie, which makes it attractive to genre buyers looking for something that can play both scary and human.

items.area: The mythology explanation arrives in a block.
items.detail: Once Gage starts explaining the shadow creatures and the portal history, the script shifts into exposition mode for a stretch. It’s clear enough to follow, but buyers will notice that the lore is delivered more as a briefing than as a dramatic reveal.

items.area: The creature design is effective but familiar.
items.detail: The light-sensitive shadow beings are a strong hook, but the movie still lives in a recognizable creature-feature lane. That makes the execution and packaging matter a lot, because the concept’s freshness comes from presentation more than from a wholly new monster grammar.

items.area: The ensemble size narrows the casting conversation.
items.detail: This is not a two-hander; it asks for a credible adult ensemble, a child performer, and specific identity casting for Sooni and the family units. That’s manageable, but it means the package benefits from strong attachments or a director with a clear ensemble track record.

items.area: The snow and night work will add friction.
items.detail: The script leans hard on blizzard conditions, dark exteriors, and repeated flashlight choreography. That keeps the movie visually coherent, but it also means weather control, night scheduling, and safety planning will be real production conversations.

items.area: The folklore material needs a legal pass.
items.detail: The Nalusa Falaya references and the Native American folklore book are specific enough to warrant an IP and cultural review before greenlight. It’s not a clearance blocker on its face, but it is a real business-affairs item because the script uses named folklore as plot infrastructure.

issues.headline: The main development conversation is the exposition load around the shadow-creature mythology, followed by the practical realities of a snowbound ensemble horror shoot. None of these are fatal, but they are the places a producer will focus when deciding whether this is a clean buy or a package-dependent one.
